statement: No secrets in source — vault only, never in git
body: Keys, tokens and connection strings load from a secret store or env at runtime, never committed (including .env). Rotate on any suspected exposure.
rationale: A committed secret is a permanent breach vector — git history keeps it after deletion.

statement: Never log tokens or PII, even at debug level
body: Redact credentials, session tokens and personal data before logging. Assume debug logs reach a shared aggregator.
rationale: Debug logs leak to aggregators and screenshares; a logged token is a live credential.

statement: Validate and parameterize every external input
body: Treat request bodies, query params and third-party payloads as hostile: validate shape, use parameterized queries, never string-concat SQL/shell.
rationale: Injection (SQLi, command, XSS) is the top OWASP class and is fully preventable at the boundary.

statement: Enforce authz on every boundary, fail closed
body: Check authorization at each entry point (route, RPC, job). On any doubt deny; never default-allow on a missing/!unknown role.
rationale: Broken access control is OWASP A01; fail-open defaults are how it ships.

statement: Write the failing test first, watch it fail
body: Red before green: add a test that fails for the missing behavior, confirm the failure is the expected one, then write minimal code to pass.
rationale: A test you never saw fail proves nothing — it may assert the wrong thing.

statement: Every change ships with a test
body: Features, bug fixes and refactors land with a test that would fail on regression. No test, no merge.
rationale: Tests catch model hallucinations and regressions before production.

statement: Assert real behavior, not a mock or fallback
body: A test must fail if the feature is broken. Never assert the value a fallback/dummy would also return; assert the real resolved result.
rationale: Green tests that assert a mock/fallback pass whether the feature works or not.

statement: Never merge on red
body: Keep the pipeline green: a failing build or test stops the line. Fix or revert before landing anything else.
rationale: A red trunk blocks everyone and hides new failures.

statement: No unwrap/expect on the request path
body: Propagate with ? and typed errors; reserve unwrap/expect for tests and truly-unreachable invariants with a comment.
rationale: An unwrap on a fallible path is a panic = a 500 or a crashed task in production.

statement: Clippy-clean: zero warnings
body: cargo clippy passes with no warnings; deny in CI. Fix, don't #[allow], unless justified with a comment.
rationale: Warnings accrete into noise that hides real issues.

statement: Fail closed on safety and identity
body: On a fallible lookup for auth/identity/money, return an error — never fabricate a default or synthesize an id.
rationale: A plausible fake on a failure path is indistinguishable from a real result and corrupts trust.

statement: Strict types — no any
body: tsconfig strict on; model real shapes. Use unknown + narrowing at boundaries instead of any.
rationale: any disables the one guarantee the type system offers.

statement: No default exports in shared packages
body: Named exports only in shared libs — stable names, better refactors and tree-shaking.
rationale: Default exports rename freely and defeat find-references.

statement: Server state through the query layer, never a store
body: Fetch/cache server data in the data/query layer; keep Svelte stores for UI state only.
rationale: Server state in a store drifts from the source of truth and races.

statement: Accessibility on every interactive element
body: Labels, roles and keyboard paths on controls; run the a11y linter. No click-only affordances.
rationale: a11y is a baseline, not a polish step; retrofitting is costly.

statement: Done means verified against live data, not the code path
body: Don't declare done on the strength of the code alone — query the real rows/artifact that prove the claim.
rationale: A premature done ships an unmet requirement; the gap surfaces later at higher cost.

statement: Verify the outcome, never a masked wrapper
body: Confirm the real result, not a wrapper that can hide it — a piped exit code, a grep count, a tail. Read the actual status/effect.
rationale: A false green ships a defect: a failing build reported as passing is the top FTR killer.

statement: Keep changes small and single-purpose
body: One concern per change; short-lived branches; integrate to trunk continuously.
rationale: Small changes review honestly, revert cleanly and keep lead time short.

statement: Make it safe to question the AI
body: Surface the assistant's uncertainty and mistakes early; never rubber-stamp generated output — a human reviews before it lands.
rationale: A generative culture (DORA) catches model errors before production.

statement: Strong fundamentals first — AI amplifies what you already are
body: Tests, small steps and clear direction turn AI into a multiplier; weak fundamentals make it a chaos engine.
rationale: Strong fundamentals + AI = extraordinary; weak + AI = more chaos, faster.

statement: Intention-revealing names
body: A name states why a thing exists and how it's used. No abbreviations or single letters outside a tiny scope; rename freely as intent clarifies.
rationale: Code is read far more than written; a good name removes the need for a comment.

statement: Small functions that do one thing
body: A function does one thing at one level of abstraction. Extract until each does a single, nameable job.
rationale: Small single-purpose functions are testable, reusable and read top-to-bottom.

statement: Command-query separation — no hidden side effects
body: A function either returns a value (query) or changes state (command), not both. A getter that mutates surprises every caller.
rationale: Hidden side effects break the reader's mental model and cause action-at-a-distance bugs.

statement: Comments explain why, not what
body: Prefer expressive code over a comment. When you do comment, justify a decision or warn of a consequence — never restate the code.
rationale: A what-comment rots out of sync with the code and misleads; a why-comment carries intent the code can't.

statement: DRY — extract, don't duplicate
body: One authoritative place for each piece of knowledge. Three near-identical copies are a refactor, not a fourth paste.
rationale: Duplication multiplies the cost of every future change and drifts out of sync.

statement: Single responsibility — one reason to change
body: A module/class/function answers to one actor and changes for one reason. Split when two concerns share a unit.
rationale: Multiple responsibilities couple unrelated changes and make every edit risky.

statement: Depend on abstractions, not concretions
body: High-level code depends on an interface/trait, not a concrete implementation; inject the concrete at the edge (DIP).
rationale: Inverting dependencies keeps the core testable and swappable without touching it.

statement: Open for extension, closed for modification
body: Add behavior via new types/config, not by editing stable, tested code (OCP). Prefer strategy/polymorphism over growing conditionals.
rationale: Editing working code to add a case risks regressions in what already ships.

statement: Composition over inheritance
body: Assemble behavior from small collaborating pieces rather than deep class hierarchies; inherit only for genuine is-a with a stable base.
rationale: Deep hierarchies are rigid and leak base-class changes across unrelated subclasses.

statement: YAGNI — build the simplest thing that meets the requirement
body: Solve the requirement in front of you; don't add speculative generality, hooks or config for imagined futures.
rationale: Speculative flexibility is carried cost and usually guesses the future wrong.

statement: Data minimization — collect only what the feature needs
body: Capture the least personal data required, keep it only as long as the purpose lasts, and delete on expiry.
rationale: Data you never hold can't leak, be subpoenaed, or fall out of retention policy.

statement: Establish a lawful basis + consent before processing personal data
body: Have a documented lawful basis (consent, contract, legitimate interest) before collecting or processing; make consent specific and revocable.
rationale: Processing without a basis is the core GDPR/privacy violation and voids downstream use.

statement: Encrypt regulated data at rest and in transit
body: TLS in transit; encryption at rest for PII/PHI/cardholder data; manage keys in a vault, never in code.
rationale: Encryption is the baseline control every regime (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI, SOC 2) expects.

statement: Audit access to regulated data
body: Record who accessed what regulated data and when, in a tamper-evident trail; review anomalies.
rationale: An access trail is required for breach investigation and every compliance audit.

statement: Honor data-subject rights (access, erasure, portability)
body: Build the paths to export, correct and delete a person's data on request within the mandated window.
rationale: These rights are legally enforceable; bolting them on later is far costlier.

statement: Accessibility is a requirement, not a polish step
body: Meet WCAG 2.1 AA: labels, roles, keyboard paths, focus order, contrast. Run the a11y linter in CI.
rationale: a11y is a baseline (and often a legal one); retrofitting it is expensive and partial.

statement: Give clear feedback for every action
body: Every action shows its state — loading, success, and a specific, actionable error. No silent operations.
rationale: Feedback is how users build a correct model of the system; silence reads as broken.

statement: Prevent errors; make the rest recoverable
body: Design to avoid mistakes (constraints, sensible defaults); for destructive actions require confirmation or offer undo.
rationale: Preventing and recovering from errors beats explaining them after the fact.

statement: Consistency over novelty
body: Reuse established patterns, components and wording; match platform conventions. Don't reinvent a control that exists.
rationale: Consistency lets users transfer what they already know; novelty taxes every interaction.

statement: Respect the user's time
body: Minimize required input, default the obvious, remember prior choices, and keep the primary path short.
rationale: Every extra field or step loses users; the fastest correct path wins.

statement: Prefer the simplest design that passes the tests
body: Prefer the simplest design that passes the tests.

statement: Refactor continuously, not in a separate phase
body: Refactor continuously, not in a separate phase.

statement: Keep changes small and single-purpose
body: Keep changes small and single-purpose.

statement: Match the house style over a new idiom
body: Match the house style over a new idiom.

statement: Reuse before a 4th near-duplicate
body: Reuse before a 4th near-duplicate.

statement: Measure, then keep what helps
body: Try a practice, measure its effect, keep it if it moves the number, drop it if it does not. No practice is sacred — the data decides.
rationale: The core loop: practices earn their place by measured impact, not by tradition.

statement: The right thing beats more things
body: Better velocity is about direction, not raw speed. Ask of any change: is this the code that does what the user needs?
rationale: Guards against shipping fast in the wrong direction.

statement: Strong fundamentals first — AI amplifies whatever you already are
body: Tests, small changes, and clear direction make AI a multiplier instead of a chaos engine.
rationale: Strong fundamentals + AI = extraordinary; weak fundamentals + AI = more chaos.

statement: Make it safe to question the AI
body: A generative culture surfaces the assistant's mistakes early; nobody rubber-stamps a model's output.
rationale: The 5th DORA key (generative culture) applied to human+AI pairing.

statement: Every change ships with a test
body: Every change ships with a test.
rationale: Tests catch AI hallucinations before production.

statement: Never merge on red
body: Never merge on red.

statement: A human reviews AI-written code before it lands
body: A human reviews AI-written code before it lands.

statement: Integrate to trunk continuously
body: Integrate to trunk continuously.

statement: Keep change lead time short
body: Keep change lead time short (commit to production in hours).

statement: Daily plan and weekly review/retro in plain language
body: Daily plan and weekly review/retro in plain language.

statement: Review with the Perfection Game
body: Review with the Perfection Game ("what would make this a 10?").

statement: Keep the pipeline green and fast
body: Keep the pipeline green and fast (a broken pipeline stops the line).

statement: Automate the deploy so shipping is boring and on-demand
body: Automate the deploy so shipping is boring and on-demand.

statement: Big-picture backlog
body: Goals across time (last quarter, this month, next half), each with a why-it-matters, not a pile of tickets.

statement: Plain English over jargon
body: Say what you mean (sensei's own insight copy follows this).

statement: Sustainable pace
body: The loop only compounds if it is still turning next month.

statement: Question whether the code needs to exist at all.
body: Before writing, ask if the requirement is real and needed now. Prefer deleting or not writing over adding. Do not build for imagined future needs — add it when a real second caller appears.
rationale: The cheapest, most correct, most secure code is the code you never write.
remediation: State the concrete requirement the code serves; if you cannot, cut it.

statement: Reuse what already exists before writing something new.
body: Search the codebase and its libraries for an existing function, type, or pattern that already does this. Three near-identical lines are a sign to refactor, not a reason to add a fourth.
rationale: Duplication is debt; reuse compounds quality and shrinks the surface to maintain.
remediation: Run sensei `search` / `get_duplicates` before adding; if a shared implementation exists, call it.

statement: Prefer the standard library over a new dependency.
body: Reach for the language/runtime standard library first. Add a third-party dependency only when it clearly earns its weight over what the stdlib already provides.
rationale: Every dependency is a maintenance, supply-chain, and security surface.
remediation: Justify a new dependency against the stdlib equivalent; prefer the stdlib when parity is close.

statement: Prefer native platform features over a library.
body: Use built-in language, runtime, and framework capabilities before pulling a package (e.g. native fetch over an HTTP client, platform CSS over a styling framework when it suffices).
rationale: Fewer moving parts; less to break, patch, and ship.
remediation: Check for a native/built-in way first; adopt a library only where the platform genuinely falls short.

statement: Choose the minimal solution — one line over fifty; no unrequested abstraction.
body: Solve the actual problem in front of you. Do not add layers, configuration, or generality nobody asked for. Add an abstraction when there is a real second caller, not in anticipation of one.
rationale: Abstraction has a carrying cost; premature generality is harder to read, change, and verify.
remediation: Prefer the smallest change that meets the acceptance criteria; introduce structure only when duplication or a concrete second use demands it.

statement: Keep the diff as small as the change requires.
body: Touch only what the task needs. Avoid drive-by rewrites, reformatting, and unrelated refactors in the same change.
rationale: Small diffs review cleanly, revert cleanly, and localize blame.
remediation: Split unrelated improvements into their own change; keep this one focused.
